Section 01

What is Spec-Driven Development?

Spec-Driven Development (SDD) is an emerging software development paradigm that has gained significant traction alongside AI-powered code generation tools. At its core, SDD inverts the traditional developer workflow.

Traditional Development

Think → Code → Test → Refine

Spec-Driven Development

Think → Specify → Generate → Validate

In SDD, the specification becomes the primary artifact, not the code. The developer's job shifts from writing code to writing precise, unambiguous specifications that an AI system can consume to produce correct, working code.

Code generation is becoming commoditized. Intent expression is not.

Why SDD Has Gained Wide Adoption

DriverExplanation
AI code quality improvedLLMs now generate production-quality code for many common patterns
SpeedGenerating code from a spec is vastly faster than writing it by hand
ConsistencyAI-generated code follows style guides and patterns uniformly
AccessibilityNon-traditional developers (PMs, designers) can participate more directly
Cost reductionLess developer time per feature means lower cost per unit of output

The SDD Ecosystem in Practice

  • Markdown files (.md) as the primary specification format
  • Prompt templates that structure how specs are fed to AI
  • Context files (like CLAUDE.md, cursor_rules) that give AI agents persistent project knowledge
  • Review cycles where humans validate AI output against the spec
Section 02

The "Death by Markdown" Problem

SDD was supposed to solve the bottleneck of code production. And it did. But SDD introduced a new bottleneck: specification production. Writing a good spec is hard — it requires deep product understanding, anticipation of edge cases, awareness of system constraints, and clear, unambiguous language.

The "AI Writing Specs" Escape Attempt

Faced with this difficulty, teams naturally asked: "If AI can write code from specs, why can't AI also write the specs?" So people started using AI to generate the specifications themselves. This creates a compounding problem: 

Vague Human Intent
       ↓
  AI-Generated Spec (Markdown)     ← May not match true intent
       ↓
  AI-Generated Code                ← Faithful to spec, but spec may be wrong
       ↓
  Output that looks right but may be subtly wrong

The AI-generated spec appears thorough — well-formatted, comprehensive-looking, using all the right terminology. But it may hallucinate requirements, miss critical edge cases, contradict existing system behavior, or use ambiguous language.

The Shifted Bottleneck

Instead of reviewing code to check if it's correct, developers must now review massive markdown documents to check if the specification is correct. The bottleneck didn't disappear. It multiplied.

ProblemExplanation
Spec review is cognitively expensiveReading a 20-page spec and verifying it matches your vague mental model is exhausting
Specs are deceptively readableAI-generated markdown reads well, making you feel like it's correct even when it isn't
No compiler for specsCode has compilers, linters, type-checkers, and tests. Specs have human eyeballs.
Specs lack execution feedbackYou can run code and see if it works. You can't "run" a spec.
Compounding errorsIf you miss a spec error, it propagates into code, tests, and docs — all consistently wrong

The Problem Stack

Problem 1 Solved

Code production was the bottleneck.
Solution: SDD + AI code generation. Result: Code production is now cheap & fast.

Problem 2 Attempted

Writing good specs is hard.
Solution: Use AI to generate specs too. Result: Specs are produced fast but may be wrong in subtle, hard-to-detect ways.

Problem 3 Unsolved

Now we must review specs AND code.
"Death by Markdown" — shifted bottleneck, not solved it. This is what SDD-Compiler proposes to address.

Root Cause

There is no "compiler" for specs. No automated system validates whether a specification actually matches human intent, is internally consistent, and aligns with the existing product's reality.

Section 03

The Vocabulary Spectrum Trap

SDD specs are vague and free-form by nature. Unlike code, which has strict vocabulary (if, else, for, while, function names), natural language specifications are inherently ambiguous. But if we enforce strict vocabulary on specifications, we inevitably slide toward creating another programming language — defeating the entire purpose of SDD.

VAGUE
Natural Language
✅ Easy to write
❌ Ambiguous ???
Constrained NL
The sweet spot? PRECISE
Programming Language
✅ Unambiguous
❌ Hard to write

The Vocabulary Trap: Any attempt to make specifications precise enough for machines to compile will, if taken to its logical conclusion, converge toward a programming language — thereby recreating the exact problem SDD was designed to solve.

Section 04

Prior Attempts at Strict Specifications

The vocabulary trap has been sprung many times before. Studying these attempts reveals what works, what fails, and why.

Formal Specification Languages (1970s–2000s)

Z Notation, VDM, TLA+, Alloy, B Method — mathematically rigorous specification languages.

Verdict: Extremely precise but almost nobody used them outside academia. Became a programming language for mathematicians.

UML / Model-Driven Architecture (1990s–2010s)

Visual specification language with the dream of generating code directly from diagrams.

Verdict: Shifted complexity from text to diagrams. Did not reduce it. Diagram-code sync was a nightmare.

BDD / Gherkin Syntax (2000s–present)

Constrained natural language (Given/When/Then) for writing executable specifications.

Verdict: Most successful attempt. Found a useful niche but couldn't generalize to full product specification.

Design by Contract — Eiffel (1986–present)

Embedded specifications (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) directly into code.

Verdict: Made code more self-documenting but didn't help non-coders specify intent.

Structured Prompt Engineering (2023–present)

Frameworks like CRISP, RACE, CO-STAR, LMQL, Guidance, BAML — systematizing how prompts are structured.

Verdict: Useful tools, wrong level of abstraction. They optimize the AI interface, not the human intent discovery process.

The Key Lesson: No fixed point on the vocabulary spectrum works for all situations. The right level of precision depends on the context, the domain, the team, and the specific requirement being expressed.

Section 05

Reframing the Problem

The word "compiler" implies well-defined input syntax. But we just established that enforcing well-defined syntax leads to the vocabulary trap. So the metaphor of a compiler may be misleading. What is the fundamental problem?

A human has a vague, incomplete, partially contradictory mental model of what they want. We need a process that converges this fuzzy intent into a precise, validated, implementation-ready specification — without requiring the human to learn a formal language.

Fundamental Requirements

RequirementDescription
R1: Intent DiscoveryHumans don't fully know what they want. The system must help them discover their intent, not just document it.
R2: Ambiguity ResolutionNatural language is inherently ambiguous. The system must detect ambiguity and resolve it through interaction, not vocabulary enforcement.
R3: Consistency ValidationNew specs must not contradict existing product behavior, previous decisions, or each other.
R4: Progressive FormalizationStart vague, get precise incrementally. Don't demand precision upfront.
R5: Executable FeedbackThe only way to truly validate a spec is to see its consequences — generated tests, prototypes, simulations.
R6: Learning / MemoryEach completed cycle should make the system smarter about this specific product.

Better Metaphors Than "Compiler"

🧑‍💻 Senior Engineer Pair Partner

Asks probing questions, points out contradictions, suggests patterns, sketches prototypes, and remembers everything. The specification emerges from dialogue.

🔍 Type Inference Engine

Let humans express intent loosely. Infer detailed requirements from context. Flag when inferences conflict. Ask the human to disambiguate only when necessary.

🧪 Test-Driven Spec

Instead of abstract requirements, provide concrete examples. The system generalizes, generates counter-examples, and you confirm or deny — progressively refining the spec.

The Reframed Technical Problem

Build a system that:

1. ACCEPTS vague natural language input
   (no strict vocabulary required)

2. CONVERGES toward precise specifications through
   multi-turn interaction (not single-pass compilation)

3. GROUNDS every specification element in something
   verifiable: a test case, a code sketch, a counter-example,
   or a reference to existing product behavior

4. VALIDATES consistency against a growing knowledge
   base of the product's history, decisions, and constraints

5. LEARNS from each completed cycle to become more
   effective at intent discovery for THIS product

The output is NOT a markdown document.
The output is a VALIDATED SPECIFICATION GRAPH:
a structured, interconnected, tested set of
requirements with full traceability.

Three Fundamental Technical Pillars

Pillar 1: Interactive Convergence Engine

How do you systematically narrow vague intent into precise specification through dialogue? What questions should be asked and in what order? When is a specification "converged enough"?

Territory: dialogue systems, active learning, information-theoretic question selection

Pillar 2: Grounding & Validation Mechanism

How do you check that a spec element is meaningful and consistent? Can you generate executable artifacts from partial specs to provide feedback? Can you detect conflicts with existing product state?

Territory: constraint satisfaction, knowledge graphs, code/test generation

Pillar 3: Product-Specific Learning Loop

How does the system accumulate knowledge about THIS product over time? How do real-world outcomes feed back? How do you represent product knowledge for retrieval and reasoning?

Territory: RAG, episodic memory, knowledge graphs, fine-tuning

Section 06

SDD-Compiler Architecture

Core Concept: The Specification Graph

Just as CMake parses source files and builds a dependency graph of targets, sources, and build rules before any compilation happens, the SDD-Compiler parses free-form human input and builds a specification graph of requirements, dependencies, and constraints before any code generation happens.

CMakeLists.txt
→
cmake
→
Dependency Graph
→
make
→
Compiled Binary
Free-form Spec
→
SDD-Compiler
→
Spec Graph
→
AI Agent
→
Generated Code

Graph Structure

SPECIFICATION GRAPH (Directed Acyclic Graph)

  Nodes  = Individual atomic requirements
  Edges  = Dependencies, derivations, and constraints between requirements
  Layers = Formal strata that organize nodes by abstraction level

  Properties of each node:
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  id:          unique identifier     │
  │  content:     the requirement text  │
  │  layer:       which formal layer    │
  │  status:      draft|validated|conflict│
  │  author:      who wrote it          │
  │  source_text: original free-form    │
  │  depends_on:  [node_ids]            │
  │  conflicts:   [node_ids]            │
  │  family:      grouping cluster      │
  └─────────────────────────────────────┘

Dual-View Architecture

The graph serves two fundamentally different consumers:

👤 Human View (Collapsed)

Nodes grouped into families — high-level clusters that hide individual node complexity. Humans see summaries like "Password Reset (12 nodes: 10 ✅, 2 ❌)" and can drill down on demand.

🤖 Agent View (Expanded)

Every individual node with full dependency edges, conflict markers, and traceability links. AI agents consume this for code generation, conflict detection, and test synthesis.

Family Grouping Criteria (in priority order)

  1. Functional Cohesion — nodes describing the same feature/capability
  2. Layer Proximity — nodes in the same formal layer
  3. Dependency Clusters — nodes that heavily depend on each other
  4. Author Proximity — nodes written by the same person in the same session
Section 07

The Formal Layers for Code Generation

Each layer constrains the layers below it — exactly analogous to how in a build system, a library target constrains the compilation of binaries that depend on it.

L0 — Business
WHY does this exist? What value does it deliver?
Example: "Users must reset passwords without contacting support"
L1 — Functional
WHAT exactly should the system do?
Example: "User clicks 'forgot password' → receives email within 30s"
L2 — Architecture
HOW is the system structured at component level?
Example: "Password reset handled by AuthService microservice"
L3 — Interfaces
HOW do components communicate?
Example: "POST /auth/reset-password {email: string} → 202 Accepted"
L4 — Data Models
WHAT data exists and how is it structured?
Example: "PasswordResetToken {id, userId, token, expiresAt, usedAt}"
L5 — Logic
HOW does the internal logic work?
Example: "On reset request: if failedAttempts ≥ 3 AND now < lockedUntil → reject"
L6 — Tests
HOW do we verify correctness?
Example: "Test: expired token → 410 Gone"

Why This Order?

LayerWhat It DeterminesWhat It Constrains Below
L0 BusinessWhy we're building thisScopes everything below
L1 FunctionalWhat users experienceConstrains architecture choices
L2 ArchitectureWhat components existConstrains interface design
L3 InterfacesHow components talkConstrains data model design
L4 Data ModelsWhat data is storedConstrains logic implementation
L5 LogicHow logic worksConstrains what tests are needed
L6 TestsHow to verify correctnessDirect input to code generation

Dependencies are not only vertical (between layers). They can be horizontal (within a layer) and diagonal (skipping layers).

Section 08

Interaction Model & Conflict Philosophy

The Write → Compile → Inspect Cycle

✏️ Write Freely
→
🔨 COMPILE
→
📊 See Graph
→
🔍 Inspect / Fix
→
🔁 Repeat

Step 1: Write Freely

User types specs in natural language. No vocabulary restrictions. Can write one sentence or a full paragraph. Can specify which layer they're targeting or let the system infer it.

Step 2: Compile (user explicitly triggers)

AI agent processes free-form text: extracts atomic requirements as new nodes, classifies each node into a formal layer, infers dependency edges to existing nodes, assigns to families, and runs conflict detection against the full graph.

Step 3: Feedback Display (immediate)

System shows new nodes created with layer assignments, edges inferred, and status indicators:

  • ❌ CONFLICTS highlighted (no fix suggested unless user asks)
  • ⚠️ AMBIGUITIES flagged (possible multiple interpretations noted)
  • ✅ VALIDATED nodes (consistent with graph)

The Conflict Highlighting Philosophy

This encodes an important UX and workflow principle:

✅ DO

  • Highlight conflicting nodes immediately
  • Show WHY they conflict
  • Show the dependency path that creates the conflict

❌ DON'T

  • Auto-suggest fixes
  • Block the user from continuing
  • Require resolution before adding more specs

Rationale: The user may have context the system doesn't. The user may be mid-thought and doesn't want interruption. Premature fix suggestions can anchor thinking in the wrong direction. The user explicitly asks for help when ready.

Design Assumptions

AssumptionDescription
#1 — Start from scratchSDD specs are built from an empty graph
#2 — Multi-person collaborationMultiple people contribute to specs; coordination is a major requirement
#3 — Code-only scopeThis SDD-Compiler is for coding, not for business or general purposes
#4 — Serial collaborationFor simplicity, all people work on the same version, each in series; versioning conflicts ignored for now
Section 09

How AI Agents Actually Process Spec Comparison

When you ask an AI agent to compare two SDD spec documents and find inconsistencies, here's what actually happens inside the model — and why it fails.

The Cognitive Task

Finding an inconsistency requires the model to consider every statement in Spec A against every statement in Spec B — a quadratic comparison task. For 30 requirements in each spec, the model must implicitly evaluate 900 pairs. Each pair requires semantic reasoning, not just string matching. 

Easy conflict (surface-level):
  S_a: "Reset token expires after 15 minutes"
  S_b: "Password recovery links should remain active for 24 hours"
  → Model must recognize these refer to the same concept with different values

Hard conflict (multi-hop reasoning):
  S_a: "System must support 10,000 concurrent users"
  S_b: "Each password reset generates a cryptographic token using 500ms of CPU time"
  → Model must calculate: 10,000 × 1% reset rate × 500ms = potential overload
  → Requires inference across statements that share NO keywords

Known Failure Modes

Lost in the Middle

Research (Stanford/Berkeley, 2023) shows LLMs have degraded recall for information in the middle of long contexts. The model pays most attention to the beginning and end. Conflicts between the middle of Spec A and the beginning of Spec B are most likely to be missed. This is a systematic, architectural bias.

Attention Dilution at Scale

As the number of requirements grows, the model distributes attention across more pairs. Each individual comparison gets less attention, and accuracy degrades. Models are often good at finding 1–2 obvious conflicts but miss the 3rd, 4th, and 5th in the same document.

Hallucinated Conflicts

The model may invent fake conflicts due to: surface similarity traps (similar words ≠ actual conflict), over-inference (unwarranted logical leaps), or pleasing bias (you asked for conflicts, so it finds some even when there aren't any).

No Verification Mechanism

When a compiler checks types, it can prove an error exists. When an LLM checks spec consistency, it produces a probabilistic guess. It's doing pattern matching on what "looks like" a conflict based on training data, not formal verification.

Section 10

Does the Graph Actually Help?

Claim 1: Token Consumption

ApproachTotal TokensAccuracy
Monolithic (paste both specs)~8,500Medium (attention dilution)
Graph-based (naive, every pair)~25,000High (focused comparisons)
Graph-based (smart filtering)~17,500High (focused + filtered)

The graph trades tokens for accuracy. It's not about using fewer tokens. It's about using tokens more effectively.

Claim 2: Hallucination Reduction

Monolithic Comparison

"Find all conflicts in 6,000 words" = high ambiguity. Model must hold all info simultaneously, pressure to find something (pleasing bias), no structure to constrain reasoning. Output: "I found 7 conflicts" — some real, some hallucinated. You have no way to verify without reading both full specs yourself.

Graph-Based Comparison

"Do these two nodes conflict?" = low ambiguity. Much smaller input, binary question (harder to hallucinate), reasoning is auditable. If it says "conflict" you can read both nodes in 5 seconds and verify.

Key Insight: Hallucination is proportional to ambiguity of task. The graph decomposes a high-ambiguity task into many low-ambiguity tasks.

Claim 3: Conflict Detection Accuracy

Problem with MonolithicHow Graph Solves It
Ordering Bias: Conflicts between paragraph 3 and paragraph 47 are less likely to be caught than between paragraphs 46 and 47 Each pair is presented in isolation. No ordering bias.
Semantic Distance: Requirements using different terminology for the same concept are hard to connect across a long document Layer classification already identifies both as the same layer/family. They're presented together for comparison.
Multi-Hop Reasoning: Indirect conflicts require knowledge + inference, which is hard while juggling dozens of other statements Model can focus ALL its reasoning capacity on one specific pair at a time.
Completeness: Monolithic produces a list with no guarantee of completeness. You can't know what was checked. Graph provides an explicit record of which pairs were checked. Gaps are visible and auditable.

Honest Tradeoff Summary

DimensionMonolithicGraph-Based
Token cost✅ Lower❌ Higher
Latency✅ Single call❌ Multiple calls
Setup complexity✅ Zero❌ Need graph logic
Hallucination rate❌ Higher✅ Lower
Conflict accuracy❌ Degrades with size✅ Stable with size
Completeness❌ Unknown✅ Auditable
Verifiability❌ Hard to check✅ Easy to check
Scalability❌ Breaks at ~100 requirements✅ Scales well
Ordering bias❌ Significant✅ Eliminated
Implementation effort✅ Trivial❌ Significant engineering

The Deepest Insight: The Graph Is for Humans, Not AI

Common assumption: "The graph helps the AI work better."

Deeper truth: "The graph helps humans manage the AI's work."

The graph is a coordination structure, not an AI optimization.

The graph enables human oversight of the AI's reasoning process:

Without Graph

"AI, compare these specs" → "I found 5 conflicts" → "Are you sure? Did you check everything?" → "I believe so" → No way to verify.

With Graph

Each node is individually verifiable (5 seconds). Each comparison is logged and auditable. Structural visualization reveals gaps. You can challenge the AI on specific pairs it missed.

The Graph Serves Three Purposes

1. Decomposition for AI

Break a hard, open-ended task (compare two documents) into easy, closed-ended tasks (compare two statements). This is where accuracy and hallucination improvements come from.

2. Coordination for Humans

Give multiple people a shared, visual, inspectable representation of the spec state. This is where the collaboration value comes from.

3. Auditability for Trust

Create a verifiable record of what was checked, what conflicted, and what was resolved. This is where the "compiler" metaphor earns its name — compilers are trusted because their checks are systematic and complete.

This is exactly how real compilers work:

A compiler doesn't just say "your code is wrong."
It says:
  - file: auth.py, line: 47
  - error: type mismatch
  - expected: int, got: string
  - in function: validate_token()

The SDD-Compiler graph does the same for specifications:
  - node: F3
  - conflicts with: F7
  - property: token TTL
  - values: 15min vs 24hr
  - dependency impact: T1, T2 tests affected

## Part 2: Operation 1 — Atomization (Text → Nodes)

### What Does "Atomic" Mean?

Before we can extract nodes, we need a formal definition of what makes a specification **atomic**. This is not arbitrary — it has a precise theoretical basis.

```
DEFINITION:
An atomic specification is the smallest unit of intent that is
INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIABLE through a single test assertion.

LITMUS TEST:
  Can you write exactly ONE test case that fully verifies 
  this spec? 
    YES → it's atomic
    NO  → it needs further decomposition

EXAMPLES:

  NOT ATOMIC (compound):
  "The system should validate the email format and send a 
   confirmation email within 30 seconds"
  
  WHY: This requires TWO test cases:
    Test 1: invalid email format → rejection
    Test 2: valid email → confirmation sent within 30s
  
  ATOMIC (decomposed):
    Node A: "System validates email format against RFC 5322"
    Node B: "System sends confirmation email within 30 seconds 
             of valid submission"
```

### The Formal Decomposition Model

Every atomic spec, regardless of how it's worded in natural language, can be decomposed into a structured tuple:

```
ATOMIC SPEC TUPLE:

  (Entity, Property, Constraint, Condition)

  Entity:     WHAT thing is being specified
  Property:   WHAT aspect of that thing
  Constraint: WHAT the spec asserts about that property
  Condition:  UNDER WHAT circumstances (optional)

EXAMPLES:

  "Reset token expires after 15 minutes"
  → Entity:     reset_token
  → Property:   time_to_live
  → Constraint: equals(15, minutes)
  → Condition:  none (always applies)

  "After 3 failed attempts, account is locked for 1 hour"
  → Entity:     user_account
  → Property:   lock_status
  → Constraint: locked(duration=1_hour)
  → Condition:  when(failed_attempts >= 3)

  "POST /auth/reset returns 202 Accepted"
  → Entity:     endpoint(/auth/reset)
  → Property:   response_status
  → Constraint: equals(202)
  → Condition:  when(method=POST)
```

This tuple structure is the theoretical **internal representation** of each node. The free-form text is the **surface form**. The AI's job in atomization is to transform surface form into internal representation.

### Why This Tuple Matters

This is not just academic taxonomy. The tuple directly enables the later operations:

```
TUPLE FIELD        ENABLES
──────────────     ────────────────────────────────────────
Entity             Finding related nodes (same entity)
Property           Detecting conflicts (same entity + same property)
Constraint         Determining if values are compatible
Condition          Detecting conditional conflicts (overlapping conditions)
```

Two nodes **conflict** if and only if:

```
node_a.entity     == node_b.entity      (same thing)
node_a.property   == node_b.property    (same aspect)
node_a.constraint != node_b.constraint  (different assertion)
node_a.condition  OVERLAPS node_b.condition  (applicable simultaneously)
```

This is the **fundamental conflict equation** of the SDD-Compiler.

### How LLMs Actually Perform Atomization

When an LLM processes free-form text into atomic nodes, it's performing several NLP tasks simultaneously:

```
LINGUISTIC SUBTASKS IN ATOMIZATION:

1. CLAUSE SEGMENTATION
   Break compound sentences into independent clauses.
   
   "The system validates email AND sends confirmation"
   → Clause 1: "The system validates email"
   → Clause 2: "[The system] sends confirmation"
   
   Linguistic basis: dependency parsing, conjunction scope resolution
   
2. COREFERENCE RESOLUTION  
   Track what pronouns and references refer to.
   
   "AuthService handles reset. It should validate tokens."
   → "It" = AuthService
   
   Linguistic basis: coreference chains
   
3. ENTITY EXTRACTION
   Identify the technical entities being specified.
   
   "Password reset token with 32-byte cryptographic key"
   → Entities: [password_reset_token, cryptographic_key]
   
   Linguistic basis: named entity recognition (NER),
   domain-specific entity detection

4. PROPERTY-VALUE EXTRACTION
   Identify what properties are being specified and their values.
   
   "expires after 15 minutes"
   → Property: expiry_time, Value: 15_minutes
   
   Linguistic basis: relation extraction, attribute-value parsing

5. CONDITION EXTRACTION
   Identify conditional clauses and their scope.
   
   "When the user has exceeded 3 attempts, lock the account"
   → Condition: failed_attempts > 3
   → Action: lock(account)
   
   Linguistic basis: conditional clause detection,
   temporal/logical connective parsing
```

### LLM Limitations in Atomization

```
FAILURE MODE 1: GRANULARITY INCONSISTENCY
  
  Sometimes the LLM produces nodes that are too coarse:
  "User authentication and password management system 
   with email verification"
  → Should be 3+ nodes but LLM keeps it as one
  
  Sometimes too fine:
  "The button should be blue"
  "The button should be clickable"  
  "The button should have the text 'Submit'"
  → Arguably one node about button specification

  ROOT CAUSE: The LLM has no calibrated sense of what 
  granularity the user/system needs. Different projects 
  need different granularity levels.

FAILURE MODE 2: IMPLICIT REQUIREMENTS INJECTION
  
  User writes: "System should have user login"
  LLM extracts:
    Node 1: "Users can log in with email and password" ← OK
    Node 2: "System stores passwords using bcrypt"    ← HALLUCINATED
    Node 3: "Failed logins are rate-limited"          ← HALLUCINATED
    
  Nodes 2 and 3 are reasonable assumptions but the user 
  never specified them. The LLM is injecting its training 
  knowledge into the spec.

  This is EXTREMELY DANGEROUS in an SDD-Compiler because 
  the whole point is to capture HUMAN intent, not AI assumptions.

FAILURE MODE 3: ENTITY NAMING INCONSISTENCY
  
  From one paragraph, the LLM might produce:
    Node 1: entity = "reset_token"
    Node 2: entity = "password_recovery_token"
    Node 3: entity = "auth_token"
    
  Are these the same entity? Different entities? 
  The LLM may not be consistent across extractions.
  This breaks the conflict equation because entity 
  matching fails.
```

### Mitigation Strategy for Atomization

```
STRATEGY: CONSTRAINED EXTRACTION WITH ENTITY REGISTRY

1. Maintain an ENTITY REGISTRY in the graph
   - Every entity ever mentioned, with canonical name
   - Aliases: {"reset_token": ["password recovery link", 
     "reset link", "recovery token"]}

2. When extracting nodes from new text:
   a. Extract entities from text
   b. For each entity, check registry for existing match
   c. If match found: use canonical name
   d. If no match: create new entity, add to registry
   e. If ambiguous: flag as ⚠️ ambiguous, ask user

3. For properties, maintain a PROPERTY REGISTRY per entity
   - reset_token.properties: [ttl, format, length, 
     delivery_method, max_attempts]
   - When new property is detected, check if it's a 
     synonym for existing property

4. NEVER inject requirements the user didn't write
   - Extraction prompt explicitly states: "Only extract 
     what the user actually wrote. Do not add assumptions, 
     best practices, or implied requirements."
```

## Part 3: Operation 2 — Placement (Node → Layer + Family)

### Layer Classification: The Theory

Each layer corresponds to a distinct **information type** — a different category of knowledge about the system:

```
INFORMATION TYPE TAXONOMY:

Layer   Information Type     Linguistic Markers
─────   ─────────────────    ──────────────────────────────────
L0      MOTIVATION           "users need", "business requires",
        (why)                "for compliance", "to support",
                             "market demands", value language

L1      BEHAVIOR             "when user does X", "system shall",
        (what happens)       "the response should", "displays",
                             "notifies", observable actions

L2      STRUCTURE            "service", "component", "module",
        (what exists)        "microservice", "handles", "owns",
                             "delegates to", architectural nouns

L3      COMMUNICATION        "POST /api", "publishes event",
        (how they talk)      "request/response", "schema",
                             "payload", "header", protocol language

L4      STATE                "table", "entity", "field", "column",
        (what's stored)      "stores", "persists", "foreign key",
                             "nullable", data modeling language

L5      ALGORITHM            "if/then", "calculates", "iterates",
        (how it thinks)      "validates by", "hashes", "compares",
                             procedural/computational language

L6      VERIFICATION         "test:", "verify that", "assert",
        (how to check)       "should return", "expected:",
                             "given/when/then", test language
```

### Classification Approaches

There are three fundamentally different approaches, each with distinct properties:

```
APPROACH A: RULE-BASED CLASSIFICATION

  Method: Pattern matching on linguistic markers
  
  if contains("POST|GET|PUT|DELETE", "/") → L3_interfaces
  if contains("table|entity|field|column") → L4_data_models
  if contains("test:|verify|assert") → L6_tests
  if contains("service|component|module") → L2_architecture
  
  ✅ Fast, deterministic, zero cost
  ✅ Transparent (you can see why it classified)
  ❌ Brittle (misses anything without keywords)
  ❌ Can't handle ambiguous cases
  ❌ Requires manual rule maintenance
  
  ACCURACY: ~60-70% for well-written specs
            ~30-40% for vague or creative language


APPROACH B: EMBEDDING-BASED CLASSIFICATION

  Method: 
  1. Compute embedding of new node
  2. Compare to centroid embedding of each layer
  3. Assign to nearest layer
  
  Layer centroids are computed from existing classified nodes:
  
  centroid_L0 = mean(embeddings of all L0 nodes)
  centroid_L1 = mean(embeddings of all L1 nodes)
  ...
  
  classification = argmin(distance(new_embedding, centroid_Lk))
  
  ✅ Handles novel language (no keyword dependency)
  ✅ Improves as more nodes are classified (centroids refine)
  ❌ Requires initial seed data (cold start problem)
  ❌ Embedding similarity ≠ layer membership
  ❌ Can be confused by cross-layer language
  
  ACCURACY: ~70-80% with good seed data
  
  COLD START PROBLEM:
  At the beginning, no nodes exist, so no centroids.
  Need pre-computed "reference centroids" from example specs.


APPROACH C: LLM-BASED CLASSIFICATION

  Method: Ask the LLM directly with definitions and examples
  
  "Given these layer definitions [L0-L6] and these examples, 
   classify this node: '...'"
  
  ✅ Highest accuracy for nuanced cases
  ✅ Can explain its reasoning
  ✅ Handles ambiguity by picking best fit
  ❌ Cost: API call per node
  ❌ Non-deterministic (may classify differently each time)
  ❌ Can be wrong with high confidence
  
  ACCURACY: ~85-95% with good few-shot examples
```

### The Recommended Hybrid: Cascade Classification

```
CASCADE CLASSIFICATION ALGORITHM:

Input: node_text
Output: layer_assignment, confidence

Step 1: RULE-BASED CHECK (cost: zero)
  Apply keyword patterns
  If STRONG match (3+ markers for same layer):
    → Return layer, confidence=HIGH
  If WEAK match (1-2 markers):
    → candidate_layer = matched layer, continue to Step 2
  If NO match:
    → continue to Step 2

Step 2: EMBEDDING CHECK (cost: minimal, local computation)
  Compute embedding of node_text
  Compare to layer centroids
  If nearest centroid distance < threshold:
    If agrees with Step 1 candidate: 
      → Return layer, confidence=HIGH
    If disagrees: 
      → continue to Step 3
  If nearest centroid distance > threshold:
    → continue to Step 3 (ambiguous)

Step 3: LLM CLASSIFICATION (cost: API call)
  Only invoked for ambiguous cases (~15-20% of nodes)
  Ask LLM with full layer definitions + few-shot examples
  → Return layer, confidence=LLM_REPORTED

COST PROFILE:
  ~70% of nodes resolved at Step 1 (zero cost)
  ~15% resolved at Step 2 (minimal cost)
  ~15% require Step 3 (API cost)
  
  Average cost per node: much lower than classifying 
  everything with LLM
```

### Family Assignment

Family assignment is a **clustering problem**, not a classification problem. Unlike layers (which have fixed, predefined classes), families emerge organically from the content.

```
FAMILY ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM:

Input: new_node (with entity extracted)
Output: family_name (existing or new)

Step 1: ENTITY MATCH
  Check if new_node's primary entity matches any entity 
  in an existing family.
  
  new_node.entity = "reset_token"
  existing families:
    "Password Reset" → entities: [reset_token, reset_email, 
                                   forgot_password_link]
    "User Session"   → entities: [session, session_token, cookie]
  
  MATCH: "Password Reset" (shares reset_token)
  → Assign to "Password Reset" family

Step 2: EMBEDDING SIMILARITY (if no entity match)
  Compute embedding of new_node.content
  Compute mean embedding of each family's nodes
  If similarity > threshold:
    → Assign to most similar family
  If similarity < threshold:
    → Create new family

Step 3: FAMILY NAMING (if new family created)
  Ask LLM: "These nodes seem to form a group. 
  Suggest a 2-3 word family name: [node contents]"
  → Return family name
```

## Part 4: Operation 3 — Linking (Finding Related Nodes)

This is the most theoretically rich and practically important operation. When a new node enters the graph, we must find **all existing nodes that are meaningfully related** to it.

### What Does "Related" Mean? A Taxonomy

Not all relationships are the same. There are distinct types of relatedness:

```
RELATIONSHIP TYPES:

TYPE 1: DEPENDENCY (derives_from / enables)
  "Token expiry set to 15 min" DERIVES FROM "OWASP compliance"
  The existence of one node is motivated by another.
  Direction: parent → child (top layer → bottom layer)

TYPE 2: CONFLICT (contradicts)
  "Token expires in 15 min" CONFLICTS WITH "Token valid for 24hr"
  Two nodes assert incompatible things.
  Direction: bidirectional (symmetric)

TYPE 3: ELABORATION (refines / details)
  "System sends reset email" is ELABORATED BY 
  "Email uses SendGrid API via async queue"
  One node provides more specific detail about another.
  Direction: general → specific (usually same or adjacent layers)

TYPE 4: CONSTRAINT (limits / shapes)
  "10,000 concurrent users" CONSTRAINS "500ms token generation"
  One node imposes limits that affect the feasibility of another.
  Direction: constraining → constrained (often cross-layer)

TYPE 5: CO-REFERENCE (mentions same entity)
  "Reset token stored in Redis" and "Reset token contains userId"
  Both reference the same entity but specify different properties.
  Direction: none (they're siblings, not parent-child)
```

### The Multi-Signal Retrieval Architecture

No single method can reliably find all types of relationships. We need multiple signals combined through a scoring system.

```
MULTI-SIGNAL RETRIEVAL ARCHITECTURE:

              New Node
                │
     ┌──────────┼──────────┬──────────────┐
     ▼          ▼          ▼              ▼
  Signal 1   Signal 2   Signal 3      Signal 4
  ENTITY     EMBEDDING  GRAPH         LAYER
  MATCH      SIMILARITY PROXIMITY     PATTERN
     │          │          │              │
     ▼          ▼          ▼              ▼
  [scores]   [scores]   [scores]      [scores]
     │          │          │              │
     └──────────┼──────────┴──────────────┘
                ▼
         SCORE FUSION
                │
                ▼
         RANKED LIST of related nodes
                │
                ▼
         TOP-K SELECTED for detailed comparison
```

### Signal 1: Entity Match

```
ENTITY MATCH ALGORITHM:

Purpose: Find nodes that reference the SAME THING

Method:
  1. Extract entities from new node using tuple decomposition
     new_node → entity: "reset_token", property: "ttl"
     
  2. For each existing node, check entity registry
     Search for nodes where:
       node.entity == new_node.entity  (exact match)
       OR node.entity ∈ aliases(new_node.entity)  (alias match)
     
  3. Score:
     exact_match → score = 1.0
     alias_match → score = 0.8
     no_match    → score = 0.0

Strengths:
  ✅ Highest precision for conflict detection
  ✅ Directly enables the conflict equation
  ✅ Fast (dictionary lookup)

Weaknesses:
  ❌ Depends entirely on entity registry quality
  ❌ Misses entities referred to with novel language
  ❌ Cannot detect INDIRECT relationships
     (where entities don't match but there's a logical connection)

DATA STRUCTURE: Inverted Entity Index

  entity_index = {
    "reset_token": ["F3", "F7", "D1", "T1", "T2"],
    "user_account": ["F4", "D2", "LG1"],
    "auth_service": ["A1", "A2", "I1"],
    "email": ["F2", "A2"],
    ...
  }
  
  Lookup time: O(1) per entity
  Returns: all node IDs mentioning that entity
```

### Signal 2: Embedding Similarity

```
EMBEDDING SIMILARITY ALGORITHM:

Purpose: Find nodes that are SEMANTICALLY CLOSE in meaning

Method:
  1. Every node in the graph has a pre-computed embedding vector
     embedding_db = {
       "F3": [0.23, -0.11, 0.87, ...],   // 768 or 1536 dimensions
       "F7": [0.25, -0.09, 0.85, ...],
       "A1": [-0.45, 0.33, 0.12, ...],
       ...
     }
     
  2. Compute embedding of new node
     new_embedding = embed(new_node.content)
     
  3. Compute cosine similarity with ALL existing nodes
     for each existing_node:
       sim = cosine(new_embedding, existing_embedding)
     
  4. Score = cosine similarity value (range: -1 to 1, typically 0 to 1)

COSINE SIMILARITY FORMULA:
                    A · B          Σ(aᵢ × bᵢ)
  cos(θ) = ───────────────── = ─────────────────────
             ||A|| × ||B||     √Σ(aᵢ²) × √Σ(bᵢ²)


Strengths:
  ✅ Catches semantic relationships even with different vocabulary
     "reset token" ↔ "password recovery credential"
     These have high cosine similarity despite different words
  ✅ Language-agnostic (works across phrasings)
  ✅ Scales well (can use approximate nearest neighbor search)

Weaknesses:
  ❌ TOPICAL similarity ≠ SPECIFICATION relevance
  
     HIGH SIMILARITY but UNRELATED:
     "User resets their password via email link"
     "User updates their email in account settings"
     
     cosine_sim ≈ 0.82 (both about user + email + account)
     But these are completely independent features!
     
  ❌ Cannot distinguish relationship TYPES
     Similarity says "these are related" but not 
     "is it a dependency? a conflict? an elaboration?"
     
  ❌ Misses INDIRECT relationships with low textual similarity
     "System uses SQLite" ↔ "Support 10,000 concurrent writes"
     cosine_sim ≈ 0.15 (very low — different topics)
     But there's a REAL architectural constraint here!

SEARCH OPTIMIZATION:

  Brute force: O(n) comparisons for n existing nodes
  
  For large graphs, use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN):
  - FAISS (Facebook)
  - Annoy (Spotify)  
  - HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)
  
  These reduce search to O(log n) with ~95% recall
  
  For a hackathon POC with < 100 nodes: brute force is fine
```

### Signal 3: Graph Proximity

```
GRAPH PROXIMITY ALGORITHM:

Purpose: Find nodes that are STRUCTURALLY CLOSE in the 
         existing dependency graph

Intuition: If node A depends on node B, and a new node 
           is related to A, it's likely also related to B
           (and to A's other neighbors)

Method:
  1. Find ANCHOR NODES: existing nodes that share entities 
     with the new node (from Signal 1) or have high embedding 
     similarity (from Signal 2)
     
  2. From each anchor node, perform bounded graph traversal:
  
     BFS_related(anchor, max_depth=2):
       depth_0: {anchor}                    → score = 1.0
       depth_1: {anchor's direct neighbors} → score = 0.5
       depth_2: {neighbors' neighbors}      → score = 0.25
       
  3. Aggregate scores across all anchor nodes:
     If a node is reachable from MULTIPLE anchors, 
     its scores ADD UP.

EXAMPLE:

  New node: "Reset token should use UUID v4 format"
  
  Entity match finds anchor: F3 ("Reset token expires in 15min")
  
  Graph traversal from F3:
    depth 0: F3 (score = 1.0)
    depth 1: B2 (score = 0.5), D1 (score = 0.5), 
             T1 (score = 0.5), T2 (score = 0.5)
    depth 2: A1 (score = 0.25), I1 (score = 0.25)
    
  Result: the new node about UUID format is related to:
    - F3 (same entity, highest)
    - D1 (data model for token — will need format field)
    - T1, T2 (tests that may need to generate valid UUIDs)
    - B2 (OWASP requirement that motivated token design)

Strengths:
  ✅ Captures STRUCTURAL relationships the text doesn't reveal
  ✅ Finds downstream IMPACT nodes (tests, data models affected)
  ✅ Works even when language is completely different
     (D1 data model may say "PasswordResetToken entity" — 
      different phrasing, but structurally connected)

Weaknesses:
  ❌ Requires existing edges to traverse (chicken-and-egg 
     for the very first nodes)
  ❌ Can over-reach in densely connected graphs
     (everything becomes "related")
  ❌ Depends on graph quality — wrong edges propagate
     wrong proximity
     
DATA STRUCTURE: Adjacency list with bidirectional lookup

  graph_adj = {
    "F3": {"depends_on": ["B2"], "depended_by": ["D1", "T1", "T2", "A1"]},
    "D1": {"depends_on": ["F3", "I1"], "depended_by": ["T1", "T2"]},
    ...
  }
  
  Traversal time: O(branching_factor ^ max_depth)
  With max_depth=2 and avg branching=4: ~16 nodes examined
```

### Signal 4: Layer Pattern Matching

```
LAYER PATTERN ALGORITHM:

Purpose: Use knowledge about TYPICAL cross-layer relationships 
         to predict which nodes in OTHER layers are likely related

Intuition: Certain layer combinations have predictable 
           dependency patterns. A new L1 (functional) node is 
           most likely to be related to L0 (business) nodes 
           above it and L2 (architecture) nodes below it.

TYPICAL DEPENDENCY PATTERNS:

  New Node Layer    Most Likely Related Layers    Relationship Type
  ──────────────    ──────────────────────────    ─────────────────
  L0 (business)     L1 (functional)               parent → child
  L1 (functional)   L0 (business) ↑               child → parent
                    L2 (architecture) ↓            parent → child
                    L6 (tests) ↓                   parent → child
  L2 (architecture) L1 (functional) ↑             child → parent
                    L3 (interfaces) ↓              parent → child
  L3 (interfaces)   L2 (architecture) ↑           child → parent
                    L4 (data models) ↓             co-reference
  L4 (data models)  L3 (interfaces) ↑             co-reference
                    L5 (logic) ↓                   constrains
  L5 (logic)        L1 (functional) ↑             derives from
                    L4 (data models)               reads/writes
                    L6 (tests) ↓                   verified by
  L6 (tests)        L1 (functional) ↑             verifies
                    L5 (logic) ↑                   verifies

Method:
  1. Classify new node's layer
  2. Identify most likely related layers from pattern table
  3. RESTRICT search to those layers (reducing search space)
  4. Within those layers, apply Signals 1-3

Strengths:
  ✅ Dramatically reduces search space
     Instead of comparing against ALL nodes, compare against
     nodes in 2-3 relevant layers only
  ✅ Encodes structural knowledge about specifications
  ✅ Prevents false matches across unrelated layers

Weaknesses:
  ❌ May miss unusual cross-layer relationships
  ❌ Assumes layer classification is correct (error propagation)
  ❌ Patterns are heuristic, not guaranteed
```

### Score Fusion: Combining All Four Signals

```
SCORE FUSION ALGORITHM:

For each existing node, compute a combined relatedness score:

  final_score(new_node, existing_node) = 
      w₁ × entity_score        (Signal 1)
    + w₂ × embedding_score     (Signal 2)
    + w₃ × graph_proximity     (Signal 3)
    + w₄ × layer_pattern       (Signal 4)

WEIGHT CONFIGURATION (recommended starting point):

  w₁ (entity match)     = 0.40   ← highest weight because
                                    entity match is strongest 
                                    predictor of actual relationship
                                    
  w₂ (embedding sim)    = 0.25   ← good for broad recall,
                                    catching semantic relatives
                                    
  w₃ (graph proximity)  = 0.25   ← captures structural 
                                    relationships invisible to
                                    text analysis
                                    
  w₄ (layer pattern)    = 0.10   ← weak signal alone but helps
                                    break ties and filter noise

SELECTION:
  Sort all existing nodes by final_score descending
  Select top-K nodes where final_score > threshold
  
  Recommended: K = 10, threshold = 0.3

OUTPUT:
  related_nodes = [
    (node_id="F3", score=0.92, signals={entity:1.0, embed:0.85, graph:0.9, layer:1.0}),
    (node_id="D1", score=0.71, signals={entity:0.8, embed:0.60, graph:0.5, layer:0.8}),
    (node_id="T1", score=0.58, signals={entity:0.8, embed:0.40, graph:0.5, layer:0.3}),
    ...
  ]

The SIGNAL BREAKDOWN is important for auditability:
  User can see WHY each node was considered related.
  "F3 is related because: same entity (reset_token), 
   high semantic similarity, and directly connected in graph"
```

## Part 5: The Complete Pipeline — End to End

```
USER TYPES: "For improved user experience, password reset 
links should remain valid for 24 hours. Many users don't 
check email right away."

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 1: ATOMIZATION
─────────────────────
Extract atomic specs:

  Raw text → NLP decomposition:
  
  Sentence 1: "password reset links should remain valid for 24 hours"
    → Atomic: YES (single entity, single property, single value)
    → Tuple: (reset_token, ttl, equals(24_hours), none)
    → Node F7 created
    
  Sentence 2: "Many users don't check email right away"
    → Atomic: NO — this is a JUSTIFICATION, not a requirement
    → Action: attach as node.rationale, not a separate node
    
  Result: 1 new node (F7)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 2: PLACEMENT
─────────────────────
Classify layer + assign family:

  Cascade classification:
    Rule-based: "should remain valid for" → behavioral spec
                "24 hours" → concrete value
                → Candidate: L1_functional (confidence: medium)
    
    Embedding: compare to layer centroids
                → Nearest: L1_functional (distance: 0.12)
                → Agrees with rule-based → HIGH confidence
    
    LLM: not needed (both signals agree)
    
  Family assignment:
    Entity "reset_token" found in entity_index
    → Existing family: "Password Reset"
    → Assign F7 to "Password Reset" family
    
  Result: F7 placed at L1_functional, family "Password Reset"

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

STEP 3: LINKING
─────────────────────
Find related nodes:

  Signal 1 — Entity Match:
    entity_index["reset_token"] → [F3, D1, T1, T2]
    All score 1.0 on entity match
    
  Signal 2 — Embedding Similarity:
    embed("reset links valid for 24 hours")
    Cosine similarities:
      F3 ("token expires 15 min"):     0.89  ← very high
      F2 ("reset email within 30s"):   0.72
      F1 ("clicks forgot password"):   0.65
      D1 ("token entity model"):       0.58
      T1 ("test valid token"):         0.54
      T2 ("test expired token"):       0.51
      B1 ("users reset without support"): 0.48
      A2 ("email via async queue"):    0.35
      
  Signal 3 — Graph Proximity:
    Anchor: F3 (highest entity + embedding match)
    BFS from F3:
      depth 0: F3 → 1.0
      depth 1: B2(0.5), D1(0.5), T1(0.5), T2(0.5), A1(0.5)
      depth 2: I1(0.25), B1(0.25)
      
  Signal 4 — Layer Pattern:
    F7 is L1_functional
    Expected related layers: L0 (parent), L2 (child), L6 (tests)
    Boost nodes in L0, L2, L6; dampen nodes in L3, L4

## Part 6: Theoretical Properties and Guarantees

### Completeness Analysis

```
CAN THIS SYSTEM GUARANTEE FINDING ALL CONFLICTS?

Short answer: NO. Here's why, precisely:

DETECTABLE CONFLICTS (system CAN find):
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
• Direct value contradictions on same entity+property
  "Token TTL = 15min" vs "Token TTL = 24hr"
  → Entity match (Signal 1) catches this reliably

• Semantic contradictions with different wording
  "Token expires quickly" vs "Token should be long-lived"
  → Embedding similarity (Signal 2) catches this often

• Downstream inconsistencies
  Change to token TTL invalidates existing tests
  → Graph traversal (Signal 3) catches this

PARTIALLY DETECTABLE (system catches sometimes):
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
• Implicit constraints
  "Use SQLite" + "Support 100K concurrent writes"
  → Requires domain knowledge the LLM may or may not have
  → Embedding similarity won't catch this (different topics)
  → Only LLM reasoning at comparison time might catch it

• Cross-domain conflicts  
  "GDPR: delete user data on request" + "Audit log: 
   retain all user actions for 7 years"
  → Entity mismatch (user_data vs audit_log)
  → Embedding similarity is moderate
  → Requires legal/domain reasoning to see the conflict

UNDETECTABLE (system CANNOT find):
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
• Conflicts with UNSTATED assumptions
  "System handles password reset" — assumes email exists
  But no node says "all users have email"
  And later: "Support phone-only accounts"
  → The conflict is with an ASSUMED but never STATED requirement
  → No system can detect conflicts with things never written down

• Emergent conflicts  
  No two individual nodes conflict, but the COMBINATION 
  of 5 nodes together creates an impossible constraint
  → Combinatorial explosion makes exhaustive checking infeasible
  → This is equivalent to the SAT problem (NP-complete)
```

### Algorithmic Complexity

```
COMPLEXITY ANALYSIS:

Given: n = total nodes in graph, k = new nodes being added

Operation 1 — Atomization:
  LLM call: O(1) per input text
  Entity extraction: O(m) where m = text length
  Total: O(1) LLM call + O(m) parsing

Operation 2 — Placement:
  Rule-based: O(p) where p = number of patterns (~50)
  Embedding centroid: O(L) where L = number of layers (7)
  LLM fallback: O(1) per ambiguous node
  Total: O(p + L) ≈ O(1) per node

Operation 3 — Linking:
  Entity index lookup: O(1)
  Embedding similarity: O(n) brute force, O(log n) with ANN
  Graph traversal: O(b^d) where b=branching, d=max_depth
  Score fusion: O(n) to score all nodes
  Conflict check: O(K) for top-K candidates
  Total: O(n) per new node

FULL PIPELINE per compile action:
  O(k × n) where k = new nodes, n = existing graph size
  
  For typical usage: k ≈ 3-5, n ≈ 50-200
  → ~1000 operations per compile → effectively instant

SCALING CONCERN:
  At n = 10,000 nodes (large product):
  k × n = 50,000 comparisons per compile
  With ANN: k × log(n) ≈ 65 comparisons
  → Still manageable with proper data structures
```

## Part 7: How This Applies to the SDD-Compiler

```
PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTATION:

1. BUILD THE ENTITY REGISTRY FIRST
   This is the single most important data structure.
   Without consistent entity naming, Signals 1 and 3 fail.
   The entity registry should be maintained from day one.

2. EMBEDDING DATABASE IS CHEAP INSURANCE
   Pre-compute embeddings for all nodes.
   Even if entity matching catches 70% of relationships,
   embeddings catch the other 20% that use different words.

3. GRAPH EDGES ARE EARNED, NOT GIVEN
   Don't assume the graph has perfect edges from the start.
   Each edge is an assertion that two nodes are related.
   Start with entity-based edges, refine with human validation.

4. CONFLICT DETECTION IS A TWO-PHASE PROCESS
   Phase 1: RETRIEVAL — find candidate related nodes (fast, broad)
   Phase 2: COMPARISON — determine if related nodes conflict 
            (slow, precise, may require LLM reasoning)
   Don't skip Phase 1 by asking LLM to check everything.

5. THE TUPLE DECOMPOSITION IS THE KEY ABSTRACTION
   (Entity, Property, Constraint, Condition)
   This is what transforms vague text into comparable units.
   Invest in getting this extraction right.

6. AUDITABILITY IS NON-NEGOTIABLE
   For every relationship detected or missed, the system 
   should be able to show WHY — which signals contributed,
   what scores were computed, and where the thresholds were.
```

### Key Differences from Classic Data Structures

```
DIFFERENCE 1: MULTI-DIMENSIONAL SIMILARITY
══════════════════════════════════════════

Classic data structures use a SINGLE comparison function:
  BST:    compare(a, b) → less | equal | greater
  Hash:   hash(key) → bucket

SDD-Compiler uses FOUR simultaneous comparison functions:
  entity_match(a, b) → score
  embedding_similarity(a, b) → score  
  graph_proximity(a, b) → score
  layer_pattern(a, b) → score

Then FUSES them into a combined score.

No classic data structure does this natively.
The closest analog is a MULTI-INDEX DATABASE where 
you query across multiple indices simultaneously 
and merge results.

The SDD-Compiler's retrieval is most similar to:
  INFORMATION RETRIEVAL / SEARCH ENGINES
  
  Google combines:
    - BM25 text matching (≈ entity match)
    - Semantic embedding similarity (≈ Signal 2)
    - PageRank / link analysis (≈ graph proximity)
    - Domain authority (≈ layer pattern)
  
  Then fuses scores into a ranked list.
  
  The SDD-Compiler is essentially a SEARCH ENGINE 
  for specifications.


DIFFERENCE 2: INSERT HAS SIDE EFFECTS
═══════════════════════════════════════

In classic data structures, inserting a node changes 
only the structure (rebalancing, rehashing), not the 
CONTENT of existing nodes.

  BST insert: may rotate nodes but doesn't change their values
  Hash insert: may rehash but doesn't modify existing entries

In SDD-Compiler, inserting a new node can:
  ✗ Change status of existing nodes (validated → conflict)
  ✗ Add edges to/from existing nodes
  ✗ Cascade impact through the graph
  ✗ Mark downstream nodes as ambiguous

This is more like a CONSTRAINT PROPAGATION system or 
a REACTIVE DATABASE where inserting data triggers rules 
that modify other data.

Closest classic analogs:
  - RETE algorithm (rule engine)
  - TRIGGER-based databases
  - SPREADSHEET recalculation (cell update cascades)


DIFFERENCE 3: "FINDING THE RIGHT LOCATION" IS SEMANTIC
══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

In a BST, the "right location" is determined by a 
comparison function: left if less, right if greater.
The location is DETERMINED by the value.

In a hash table, the location is DETERMINED by the hash.

In the SDD-Compiler, the "right location" means:
  - Which LAYER (classification problem)
  - Which FAMILY (clustering problem)
  - Which EDGES to create (relationship detection problem)
  - Which CONFLICTS exist (constraint satisfaction problem)

None of these have a deterministic answer. They're all 
PROBABILISTIC, requiring either learned models (embeddings, 
LLM) or heuristics (rules, patterns).

The location is not DETERMINED by the value — it's 
INFERRED from the value's meaning.


DIFFERENCE 4: THE BOTTLENECK IS DIFFERENT
═════════════════════════════════════════

Classic data structures:
  Bottleneck = algorithmic complexity
  BST: O(log n) because of tree height
  Hash: O(1) amortized but O(n) worst case (collisions)
  
  The MATH is the expensive part.

SDD-Compiler:
  Bottleneck = LLM inference calls
  
  All the math (entity matching, embedding cosine, BFS, 
  score fusion) takes < 0.01 seconds for n=1000.
  
  One LLM call takes 1-3 seconds.
  
  The UNDERSTANDING is the expensive part, not the COMPUTATION.

COMPLEXITY COMPARISON:

  n nodes    BST insert   Hash insert   SDD-Compiler insert
  ────────   ──────────   ───────────   ─────────────────────
  10         ~3 ops       ~1 op         ~200 ops + 2 LLM calls
  100        ~7 ops       ~1 op         ~800 ops + 2 LLM calls
  1,000      ~10 ops      ~1 op         ~5,000 ops + 2 LLM calls
  10,000     ~13 ops      ~1 op         ~50,000 ops + 2 LLM calls
  100,000    ~17 ops      ~1 op         ~500,000 ops + 2 LLM calls
  
  But in WALL CLOCK TIME:
  
  n nodes    BST insert   Hash insert   SDD-Compiler insert
  ────────   ──────────   ───────────   ─────────────────────
  10         <1μs         <1μs          ~3 seconds
  100        <1μs         <1μs          ~3 seconds
  1,000      <1μs         <1μs          ~3 seconds
  10,000     <1μs         <1μs          ~4 seconds
  100,000    <1μs         <1μs          ~5 seconds
  
  The SDD-Compiler has FLAT-ISH wall clock time because 
  the LLM calls dominate and don't scale with n.
  The math scales linearly but is negligible compared to LLM.
```

## Optimization Strategies: Reducing the n Comparisons

```
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CAN WE AVOID COMPARING AGAINST ALL n NODES?
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

YES. Here's how each signal can be optimized:

SIGNAL 1 — ENTITY MATCH:
  Current: O(n) — score all nodes
  Optimized: O(1) — use inverted entity index
  
  entity_index["file"] → [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, F7, LG1]
  
  Instead of checking all 13 nodes, directly retrieve 
  the 7 that match. Skip the other 6 entirely.
  
  This is already what we're doing! Entity match is O(1) 
  lookup + O(m) where m = matching nodes, typically m << n.


SIGNAL 2 — EMBEDDING SIMILARITY:
  Current: O(n × D) — brute force cosine with all nodes
  Optimized: O(log n × D) — use Approximate Nearest Neighbor
  
  HNSW index (e.g., FAISS):
    Build time: O(n × log n × D) — done once, incrementally updated
    Query time: O(log n × D) — returns top-K nearest neighbors
    
  For n=1000, D=768:
    Brute force: 768,000 FLOPs
    HNSW:        ~5,000 FLOPs (150x faster)
    
  For n=100,000, D=768:
    Brute force: 76,800,000 FLOPs
    HNSW:        ~12,000 FLOPs (6,400x faster)


SIGNAL 3 — GRAPH PROXIMITY:
  Current: O(a × b^d) — BFS from each anchor
  Optimized: Already efficient for small d (=2)
  
  Further optimization: pre-compute k-hop neighborhoods
  and cache them. Update incrementally when edges change.
  
  Cache: neighborhood[F1] = {depth_1: [F4,F5,F7,A3,A1], 
                              depth_2: [F6,F2,A2,...]}
  Lookup: O(1) per anchor (cached)
  Cache update on edge insertion: O(b^d) per affected node


SIGNAL 4 — LAYER PATTERN:
  Current: O(n) — check each node's layer
  Optimized: O(L) — use layer index
  
  layer_index = {
    L1: [F1,F2,F3,F4,F5,F6,F7,F8],
    L2: [A1,A2,A3],
    L5: [LG1],
    L6: [T1]
  }
  
  Only retrieve nodes in RELEVANT layers (typically 2-3 layers).
  Skip all nodes in irrelevant layers.
  
  For a new L3 node: only look at L1 (8 nodes), L2 (3 nodes), 
  L4 (0 nodes) = 11 nodes instead of 13.
  Savings grow with graph size.


CONFLICT DETECTION:
  Current: O(K) where K = top candidates
  Optimized: Already efficient — K is fixed constant (5-10)
  
  The KEY optimization is: K does NOT grow with n.
  Even with 100,000 nodes, you only check the top 10 
  candidates for conflicts. Everything else has already 
  been filtered out by the 4 signals.


OPTIMIZED TOTAL COMPLEXITY:

  Phase              Current         Optimized
  ─────────────      ─────────       ────────────
  Entity match       O(n)            O(1) + O(m), m<<n
  Embedding sim      O(n × D)        O(log n × D) with ANN
  Graph proximity    O(a × b^d)      O(a) with cached neighborhoods
  Layer pattern      O(n)            O(L × n_per_layer)
  Score fusion       O(n log n)      O(C log C), C=candidate set<<n
  Conflict           O(K)            O(K), K is constant
  ─────────────      ─────────       ────────────
  TOTAL              O(n × D)        O(log n × D + m + a)
                     LINEAR in n     SUBLINEAR in n

  PRACTICAL MEANING:
  With optimizations, adding the (n+1)th node to a graph 
  of 100,000 nodes costs roughly the same as adding it 
  to a graph of 1,000 nodes. The bottleneck remains the 
  LLM calls, which are constant regardless of graph size.
```

# How a Fresh AI Reads a Specification Graph to Generate Code

---

## Part 1: What "Reading Specs to Generate Code" Actually Means

### The Fundamental Task

Before comparing graph vs markdown, let's understand what the AI is actually doing when it generates code from specifications. This is not a simple translation task. It's a **multi-step reasoning and synthesis task**.

```
WHAT THE AI MUST DO:

  Input:  A set of specifications describing desired behavior
  Output: A set of source code files that implement that behavior

  This requires:
  
  1. COMPREHENSION
     Understand what each spec means in terms of software behavior
     
  2. ARCHITECTURE INFERENCE
     Determine what files, classes, functions, and modules are needed
     
  3. DEPENDENCY ORDERING
     Determine what must be built first (you can't write the API 
     handler before you've defined the data model it uses)
     
  4. CODE SYNTHESIS
     Actually generate syntactically correct, logically sound code
     
  5. CROSS-FILE CONSISTENCY
     Ensure that file A imports from file B correctly, that 
     type definitions match across boundaries, that API contracts 
     are honored by both caller and callee
     
  6. COMPLETENESS VERIFICATION
     Ensure every spec is addressed in the generated code,
     nothing is forgotten
```

### How Transformers Process Text — The Mechanics

To understand why graph vs markdown matters, you need to understand how transformers actually process input at a mechanical level.

```
TRANSFORMER PROCESSING (simplified):

  Input tokens: [t₁, t₂, t₃, ..., tₙ]
  
  Self-attention layer:
    For each token tᵢ, compute attention weights to ALL other tokens:
    
    attention(tᵢ, tⱼ) = softmax(Qᵢ · Kⱼᵀ / √d)
    
    Where:
      Qᵢ = query vector for token tᵢ (what am I looking for?)
      Kⱼ = key vector for token tⱼ (what do I contain?)
      d  = dimension of key vectors
    
    The attention weight tells the model:
    "How much should token tᵢ pay attention to token tⱼ?"
    
  After computing attention weights, each token's representation 
  is updated as a weighted sum of all other tokens' values:
  
    output(tᵢ) = Σⱼ attention(tᵢ, tⱼ) × Vⱼ

KEY INSIGHT:
  The model does NOT "read" sequentially like a human.
  It processes ALL tokens simultaneously in each layer.
  But attention is a LIMITED RESOURCE — it must be 
  distributed across all input tokens.
```

### The Attention Budget Problem

This is the core insight that makes graph vs markdown a meaningful comparison.

```
ATTENTION BUDGET:

  Think of attention as a BUDGET that each token must spend 
  across all other tokens in the context window.
  
  Total attention per token = 1.0 (softmax normalizes to 1)
  
  If context has 1,000 tokens:
    Average attention per token pair = 1/1000 = 0.001
    
  If context has 10,000 tokens:
    Average attention per token pair = 1/10000 = 0.0001
    
  Of course, attention is NOT uniform. The model learns to 
  concentrate attention on relevant tokens. But there's a 
  fundamental tension:
  
  MORE TOKENS IN CONTEXT → each individual token gets 
  LESS attention on average → important relationships 
  are more likely to be MISSED or WEAKENED.
  
  This is not a theoretical concern. It's the root cause 
  of the "lost in the middle" phenomenon, long-context 
  degradation, and instruction-following failures in 
  large contexts.
```

```

### What Happens Inside the Model

```
PROCESSING FLAT MARKDOWN — STEP BY STEP:

STEP 1: The model reads ALL 514 input tokens at once.
        Every spec is in the same flat list.
        No explicit structure beyond markdown headers.

STEP 2: The model must INFER structure from the text:
  
  "Hmm, 'maximum file upload size is 100 megabytes' and 
   'enterprise customers can upload up to 5 gigabytes' — 
   these are related. One is a general limit, one is an 
   enterprise override."
   
  The model must USE ATTENTION to connect these two 
  statements, which are separated by 3 other bullet points.
  
  Attention distance: ~40 tokens apart.
  
  In a 514-token context, this is manageable.
  In a 5,000-token context with 100 specs, this gets harder.

STEP 3: The model must DECIDE what files to generate.
  
  This decision is NOT explicit in the markdown.
  The model must infer from the specs:
  
  "I see mentions of S3, PostgreSQL, FileService, 
   virus scanning, share links, signed URLs...
   I should probably create:
     - A FileService class
     - A data model for files and share links
     - API route handlers
     - An S3 utility module
     - Tests"
  
  This inference is ENTIRELY based on the model's training.
  Different runs may produce different file structures.
  
STEP 4: The model generates code TOKEN BY TOKEN.
  
  When generating line 150 of the FileService class,
  the model's context window contains:
  
  [system prompt] [all specs] [150 lines of code already generated]
  
  Total tokens: 200 + 514 + ~600 = ~1,314 tokens
  
  The model must simultaneously:
  - Remember what specs it hasn't addressed yet
  - Maintain consistency with code already generated
  - Follow language syntax rules
  - Keep track of variable names, types, imports
  
  ALL of this competes for the same attention budget.
```

### Failure Modes of Flat Markdown

```
FAILURE MODE 1: SPECIFICATION DROPOUT
═════════════════════════════════════

  The model generates code that addresses specs 1-6 
  but "forgets" specs 7-8. This happens because:
  
  As the OUTPUT grows, the attention budget is split between:
  - Input specs (need to remember what to implement)
  - Generated code (need to maintain consistency)
  
  Later specs in the list get less attention as output grows.
  
  EXPERIMENTAL EVIDENCE:
  In studies of LLM code generation from long specs, 
  requirement coverage drops significantly after 
  the first 10-15 requirements.
  
  Coverage by position in flat list:
    Spec 1-5:   ~95% implemented correctly
    Spec 6-10:  ~85% implemented correctly
    Spec 11-15: ~70% implemented correctly
    Spec 16-20: ~55% implemented correctly
    Spec 20+:   ~40% implemented correctly
  
  (These numbers are illustrative based on published 
   benchmarks like SWE-Bench and HumanEval+)


FAILURE MODE 2: CROSS-REFERENCE CONFUSION
═════════════════════════════════════════

  The model must mentally link:
    "Maximum file upload size is 100 megabytes"
    "Enterprise customers can upload up to 5 gigabytes"
    "Chunked uploading with resume capability"
    "File binary content stored in S3"
    "FileService handles all file operations"
  
  These 5 specs from 4 different sections all interact 
  in the upload handler. The model must:
  
  1. Recognize they're all relevant to the same code
  2. Synthesize them into a coherent implementation:
  
     async function uploadFile(req) {
       const maxSize = req.user.isEnterprise ? 5_GB : 100_MB;
       if (file.size > maxSize) throw new FileTooLargeError();
       if (file.size > CHUNK_THRESHOLD) {
         return chunkedUpload(file, s3Client);
       } else {
         return directUpload(file, s3Client);
       }
     }
  
  If the model fails to connect all 5 specs, it might:
  - Forget the enterprise override → only implement 100MB limit
  - Forget chunked upload → only implement direct upload
  - Forget S3 → use local filesystem
  
  The MORE specs interact, the HARDER it is for flat 
  markdown to convey these interactions.


FAILURE MODE 3: DEPENDENCY MISORDERING
═════════════════════════════════════

  The model generates files in a stream. If it writes 
  the API handler before the data model, it must either:
  
  a) GUESS what the data model will look like
     (and hope it's consistent when it generates the model later)
     
  b) BACKTRACK and rewrite the handler
     (most models don't do this in single-pass generation)
  
  Flat markdown doesn't tell the model WHAT TO GENERATE FIRST.
  The model must infer the build order from its training.
  
  If it gets the order wrong, downstream files may be 
  inconsistent with upstream files.


FAILURE MODE 4: NO VERIFICATION OF COMPLETENESS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  After generating all code, how does the model know 
  it addressed every spec?
  
  With flat markdown, there's no checklist mechanism.
  The model generates until it "feels done."
  
  It has no way to verify:
  - Did I implement virus scanning? (spec 5)
  - Did I handle link expiration? (spec 3)
  - Did I implement the 404 for expired links? (spec 12)
  
  In practice, 10-30% of specs are routinely missed 
  in single-pass generation from long flat specs.
```

## Part 3: Method B — The Graph Approach

### The Key Insight: Decomposed Generation

Instead of asking the AI to generate **everything at once** from **all specs**, the graph enables **targeted generation** where each generation call receives **only the relevant specs**.

```
FUNDAMENTAL DIFFERENCE:

  FLAT MARKDOWN:
    1 call × ALL specs × ALL code = monolithic generation
    
  GRAPH:
    N calls × RELEVANT specs per call × FOCUSED code per call
    = decomposed generation
    
  This is the SAME principle as:
    Monolithic compilation (compile entire program at once)
    vs
    Modular compilation (compile each module separately, then link)
```

### How the AI Reads the Graph

```
GRAPH-BASED CODE GENERATION — THE ALGORITHM:

STEP 1: TOPOLOGICAL SORT OF THE GRAPH
════════════════════════════════════════

  The graph has layers L0 → L6 with dependency edges.
  Perform topological sort to determine generation order.
  
  Our graph's dependency order:
  
    Level 0 (no dependencies):
      F4: Max size 100MB
      F6: Enterprise 5GB
      
    Level 1 (depends on Level 0):
      F1: Upload files (depends on F4)
      
    Level 2:
      F5: Virus scan (depends on F1)
      F7: Chunked upload (depends on F1, F6)
      
    Level 3:
      F2: Share via link (depends on F5)
      
    Level 4:
      F3: Links expire (depends on F2)
      
    Level 5:
      F8: Default 30 days (depends on F3)
      LG1: File not deleted on expiry (depends on F3)
      
    Level 6:
      I1: Signed URLs (depends on A1, A3)
      T1: Expired link → 404 (depends on F3, F8)
      
    Architecture (parallel track):
      A1: S3 storage
      A2: PostgreSQL
      A3: FileService
  
  This topological sort tells the AI:
  "Generate data models first, then services, then handlers, 
   then tests."
   
  Topological sort cost: O(V + E) = O(13 + 18) = O(31)
  This is computed ONCE before generation begins.


STEP 2: GROUP NODES INTO CODE GENERATION TASKS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════

  Each generation task produces ONE code artifact (file/module).
  The graph structure tells us which specs are relevant to 
  which artifact.
  
  TASK 1: Data Models
  ────────────────────
    Relevant nodes: A2 (PostgreSQL), F4 (max size), F6 (enterprise size),
                    F3 (link expiry), F8 (30-day default), D1 (token entity)
    Output: src/models/file.ts, src/models/shareLink.ts
    
  TASK 2: S3 Storage Module
  ────────────────────────
    Relevant nodes: A1 (S3), F4 (max size), F6 (5GB), 
                    F7 (chunked upload), I1 (signed URLs)
    Output: src/storage/s3.ts
    
  TASK 3: Upload Handler
  ───────────────────────
    Relevant nodes: F1 (upload), F4 (100MB limit), F6 (5GB enterprise),
                    F5 (virus scan), F7 (chunked upload), A3 (FileService)
    Dependencies: TASK 1 (data models), TASK 2 (S3 module)
    Output: src/services/uploadService.ts
    
  TASK 4: Share Link Handler
  ──────────────────────────
    Relevant nodes: F2 (share via link), F3 (expiry), F8 (30 days),
                    LG1 (don't delete file), I1 (signed URLs)
    Dependencies: TASK 1 (data models), TASK 2 (S3 module)
    Output: src/services/shareLinkService.ts
    
  TASK 5: API Routes
  ──────────────────
    Relevant nodes: I1 (signed URLs), F1 (upload), F2 (share),
                    T1 (expired → 404)
    Dependencies: TASK 3, TASK 4
    Output: src/routes/fileRoutes.ts
    
  TASK 6: Tests
  ─────────────
    Relevant nodes: T1 (expired link → 404), F4 (size limit),
                    F5 (virus scan), F8 (30-day validity)
    Dependencies: ALL above
    Output: tests/fileService.test.ts

  HOW ARE THESE GROUPINGS DETERMINED?
  
  Method: Subgraph extraction based on code artifact type
  
  For each target artifact:
    1. Identify the PRIMARY nodes (direct specs for this artifact)
    2. Traverse UPWARD in graph to find constraining ancestors
    3. Traverse SIDEWAYS to find sibling constraints
    4. Package these nodes as the context for generation
    
  This is analogous to how a BUILD SYSTEM resolves dependencies:
    "To compile uploadService.ts, I need the headers from 
     models/file.ts and storage/s3.ts"


STEP 3: GENERATE CODE PER TASK
══════════════════════════════

  For each task, make ONE AI call with ONLY the relevant specs.

  TASK 3 EXAMPLE (Upload Handler):
  
  AI RECEIVES:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  System prompt: "Generate TypeScript code for the upload 
  service. Use the provided data models and S3 module."
  
  Relevant specs:
    F1: "Users can upload files to the system"
    F4: "Maximum file upload size is 100 megabytes"
    F6: "Enterprise customers can upload files up to 5 gigabytes"
    F5: "Every uploaded file is virus-scanned before accessible"
    F7: "Large file uploads support chunked uploading with resume"
    A3: "FileService microservice handles all file operations"
  
  Dependencies (already generated code):
    // From models/file.ts (TASK 1 output):
    interface File {
      id: string;
      name: string;
      size: number;
      uploadedBy: string;
      scanStatus: 'pending' | 'clean' | 'infected';
      s3Key: string;
      createdAt: Date;
    }
    
    // From storage/s3.ts (TASK 2 output):
    class S3Storage {
      async upload(key: string, data: Buffer): Promise<void>;
      async uploadMultipart(key: string, stream: Readable): Promise<void>;
      async getSignedUrl(key: string, expiresIn: number): Promise<string>;
    }
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  
  AI GENERATES:
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
  // src/services/uploadService.ts
  
  const DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE = 100 * 1024 * 1024;      // 100 MB
  const ENTERPRISE_MAX_SIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024 * 1024; // 5 GB  
  const CHUNK_THRESHOLD = 100 * 1024 * 1024;         // 100 MB
  
  export class UploadService {
    constructor(
      private s3: S3Storage,
      private virusScanner: VirusScanner,
      private fileRepo: FileRepository
    ) {}
  
    async uploadFile(input: UploadInput): Promise<File> {
      const maxSize = input.user.isEnterprise 
        ? ENTERPRISE_MAX_SIZE 
        : DEFAULT_MAX_SIZE;
        
      if (input.file.size > maxSize) {
        throw new FileTooLargeError(input.file.size, maxSize);
      }
      
      // Upload to S3 (chunked for large files)
      const s3Key = generateS3Key(input.user.id, input.file.name);
      if (input.file.size > CHUNK_THRESHOLD) {
        await this.s3.uploadMultipart(s3Key, input.file.stream);
      } else {
        await this.s3.upload(s3Key, input.file.buffer);
      }
      
      // Create file record with pending scan status
      const file = await this.fileRepo.create({
        name: input.file.name,
        size: input.file.size,
        uploadedBy: input.user.id,
        scanStatus: 'pending',
        s3Key,
      });
      
      // Trigger async virus scan
      await this.virusScanner.scan(file.id, s3Key);
      
      return file;
    }
  }
  ─────────────────────────────────────────
```

     generates extra validation, error handling, or comments 
     as a "safety net" because it's uncertain about the 
     requirements. With focused specs, it's more confident 
     and generates leaner code.

## Part 5: Accuracy and Quality Comparison

### Defining Accuracy Metrics

```
METRIC 1: SPECIFICATION COVERAGE
  What percentage of specs are correctly implemented in code?
  
  Measured by: For each spec, can you find corresponding 
  code that implements it?

METRIC 2: CROSS-FILE CONSISTENCY
  Do types, interfaces, and function signatures match 
  across file boundaries?
  
  Measured by: Does the code compile? Do imports resolve?
  Do function calls match function signatures?

METRIC 3: LOGIC CORRECTNESS
  Does the generated code actually do what the spec says?
  
  Measured by: Do the generated tests pass? 
  Does manual inspection confirm correct behavior?

METRIC 4: ARCHITECTURAL COHERENCE
  Is the code organized in a sensible, maintainable way?
  
  Measured by: Code review. Are concerns separated? 
  Are dependencies clean? Is naming consistent?
```

### Specification Coverage Analysis

  A2      PostgreSQL metadata                  ✅ YES (architecture decision)

  T1      Expired link → 404                   ⚠️ PARTIAL (test may be incomplete)

    Partially covered: 4/14 = 29%
    Missed:            2/14 = 14%
